intro: Twice in American history, a secret order called the Ku Klux Klan grew into a powerful force. The first Klan rode at night in the South after the Civil War. It used terror to keep freedpeople from voting, learning and owning land. The second Klan rose in 1915 and spread across the whole country, including Illinois. It sold memberships like a lodge and targeted Black Americans, Catholics, Jews and immigrants.

This unit puts the people who fought back at the center. You will meet survivors who testified to Congress, like the teacher and preacher Elias Hill. You will meet prosecutors, reporters, a Chicago league that printed Klan members' names, a young woman whose last words convicted a Klan leader, and Ida B. Wells, who fought lynching with facts from her home in Chicago.

By the end, you will be able to explain how secrecy helped a hate group escape the law. You will be able to compare sources that disagree and sort documented facts from disputed stories. You will also weigh a hard question: when does exposing names protect people, and when does keeping names private protect them instead?
bigQuestion: How did secrecy make the Klan powerful, and what finally broke its hold?

timeline.t: Six Confederate veterans form the Ku Klux in Pulaski, Tennessee.
Congress passes the Ku Klux Klan Act and forms the Joint Select Committee.
President Grant suspends habeas corpus in nine South Carolina counties.
The committee's 13-volume report of testimony goes to Congress.
The White League forms openly in Louisiana to overturn Reconstruction.
Ida B. Wells publishes A Red Record in Chicago.
William J. Simmons launches a second Klan on Stone Mountain, Georgia.
The New York World begins its 21-day exposé of the Klan.
Chicago's American Unity League begins printing members' names in Tolerance.
A gunfight in a Herrin, Illinois, cigar store kills four men.
D. C. Stephenson is convicted of murder in Noblesville, Indiana.
NAACP v. Alabama protects the NAACP's membership lists.

words.d: the years 1865 to 1877, when the nation rebuilt the South and decided what freedom would mean
organized like an army but not an official army
violence and threats against ordinary people to reach a political goal
threats meant to make people too afraid to act
a statement made under oath
a person's right to be brought before a judge and not held in jail without cause
making people answer for what they do
the belief that people born in a country deserve more rights than newcomers
a report that reveals hidden wrongdoing
a sworn statement by a person who knows he or she is dying, which a court may accept as evidence
the right to join together with others for a shared cause
a person's written account of his or her own life and experiences

test.q: Where and by whom was the first Ku Klux formed?
choices: In Pulaski, Tennessee, by six Confederate veterans
On Stone Mountain, Georgia, by William J. Simmons
In Chicago, by the American Unity League
In Nashville, by members of Congress
test.why: The first Klan began in Pulaski, Tennessee, as a club of six Confederate veterans. Simmons founded the second Klan in 1915.

test.q: What was the main goal of the first Klan's night riding?
choices: To guard Southern towns from bandits
To keep Black citizens and their allies from voting and holding power
test.why: The first Klan used terror to stop Black citizens from voting, owning land, going to school and holding office.

test.q: Why is the Joint Select Committee's 1872 report so valuable to historians?
choices: It was written by Klan leaders
It holds the sworn testimony of hundreds of witnesses
It is a novel about Reconstruction
It lists every Klan member by name
test.why: Its 13 volumes hold sworn testimony from hundreds of witnesses, including survivors who named their attackers.

test.q: What did Elias Hill do that makes him central to this unit?
choices: He directed The Birth of a Nation
He survived a Klan attack, testified, and led neighbors to Liberia
test.why: Hill, a disabled Baptist preacher and teacher, testified about the attack and led a group of neighbors to Arthington, Liberia.

test.q: Which part of the Ku Klux Klan Act of 1871 still matters today?
choices: Section 1, which lets people sue officials who violate their constitutional rights
The rule that set the Klan's joining fee
The rule that created the NAACP
test.why: Section 1 survives as 42 U.S.C. section 1983, which the Supreme Court relied on in Monroe v. Pape, a Chicago police case.

test.q: How did the White League differ from the first Klan?
choices: It operated openly instead of in secret
test.why: The White League, founded in Louisiana in 1874, did not hide. It used violence openly.

test.q: What did The Birth of a Nation do in 1915?
choices: It glorified the first Klan and helped the second Klan recruit
It was banned everywhere before anyone saw it
test.why: The film showed the Klan as heroes, and Simmons used its fame to recruit for the new Klan.

test.q: How did the second Klan make money?
choices: Recruiters sold memberships for a $10 fee and kept a commission
It charged the government for protection
It won prize money from contests
test.why: Recruiters called Kleagles collected a $10 fee, kept a share and sent the rest up to leaders.

test.q: Which statement about where the 1920s Klan was strong is supported by the evidence?
choices: It existed only in the rural South
It was strongest in New England
It was strong in Northern cities; Chicago had about 50,000 members
test.why: The Encyclopedia of Chicago counts about 50,000 members in the Chicago area, the largest city membership in the nation.

test.q: What was a surprising result of the New York World's 1921 exposé?
test.why: Klan leaders themselves said the exposé helped them grow. It was an unintended consequence.

test.q: What was the purpose of printing names in Tolerance?
choices: To break the Klan's secrecy so members had to face their community
test.why: The American Unity League printed names so Klan members could no longer hide from their neighbors.

test.q: In the Williamson County Klan war, what do historians debate?
choices: Whether the raids were about liquor, prejudice against immigrants and Catholics, or both
Whether the Klan ever held raids
test.why: The Klan said it was enforcing Prohibition, but many of those raided were Italian immigrants and Catholics, so historians see both motives.

test.q: What brought down D. C. Stephenson?
choices: A Supreme Court ruling about the NAACP
Madge Oberholtzer's dying declaration, used as evidence at his murder trial
test.why: Her sworn statement was admitted in court, and he was convicted of second-degree murder in 1925.

test.q: Why did the Supreme Court protect the NAACP's membership list in 1958?
choices: The NAACP had broken no laws in any state
Revealing it would expose members to harm and weaken their freedom of association
The list had already been printed
Alabama asked the Court to protect it
test.why: In NAACP v. Alabama, the Court said forcing out the names would expose members to harm and weaken their freedom of association.

test.q: Which statement about Stetson Kennedy is best supported by the evidence?
choices: He had no part in fighting the Klan
He never wrote about his own role
He did real anti-Klan work, but much of his inside information came from an informant
test.why: The 2006 article Hoodwinked? reported the informant, while his defenders point to his real work against the Klan.

write.prompt: Which did more to break the Klan's power: witnesses who testified, laws and courts, or reporters who exposed it? Make a claim. Support it with two or three facts or sources from this unit, and explain why they matter.
tips: Name your sources, such as the 1872 committee report, the Ku Klux Klan Act or the New York World series.
Use unit words like testimony, accountability and exposé correctly.
Give the other side fairly before you explain why your claim is stronger.
Keep the survivors and witnesses at the center of your answer.

title: The Klan and the People Who Fought It

chapters.title: Terror in the Reconstruction South
chapters.bigQuestion: How did a secret order use terror to take away freedpeople's rights, and how did witnesses and the law fight back?

story.title: A Long Road to Washington
story.kicker: In 1871, a farmer who lived through a night raid carries his story to Congress.
paragraphs: This scene is a composite. It is built from the kinds of accounts many witnesses gave Congress in 1871. It is spring in upstate South Carolina. A Black farmer stands at the edge of his small cornfield. He is paying for the land, bit by bit. He voted in the last election. Everyone in the county knows it.

A few weeks ago, riders came in the night. Cloth hoods covered their faces. They pulled him from his cabin and whipped him in front of his children. They warned him never to vote again. Before they rode off, he heard one of them laugh. He knew that laugh. It belonged to a man who farms a few miles down the road.

Now word has come that a committee of Congress wants to hear what is happening in the South. He can go and tell his story under oath. His wife is afraid. If the riders learn that he spoke, they may come back. He thinks about it for two nights. Then he packs his one good coat.

In Washington, the room is large and full of strangers. Lawmakers sit at a long table. A clerk writes down every word. The farmer tells what he saw, in order. He names the man he recognized. It is the first time anyone in power has asked him what happened to him.

Across the South, hundreds of people made choices like his. Some spoke when the committee came to their own counties. Others traveled far. Their sworn words filled thousands of printed pages. Those pages are the main reason we know the truth about the first Ku Klux Klan today.
story.think: What risks did witnesses take by testifying, and why do you think so many chose to speak anyway?

lessons.title: After Emancipation
lessons.mainIdea: After the Civil War, new amendments made freedpeople citizens and voters, and many white Southerners were furious.
reading: The Civil War ended in 1865, and about four million enslaved people became free. The Thirteenth Amendment, ratified that December, ended slavery in the United States. An *amendment* is a formal change added to the Constitution. Freedpeople moved quickly to build their own lives. They found lost family members, founded churches, opened schools and looked for land and fair pay.

The years from 1865 to 1877 are called *Reconstruction*. During this time the nation rebuilt the South and argued over what freedom would mean. The Fourteenth Amendment (1868) made formerly enslaved people citizens. It promised every person equal protection of the laws. The Fifteenth Amendment (1870) said no citizen could be denied the vote because of race.

Each *freedperson* now had rights that had been denied for generations. Black men voted in large numbers. Hundreds served in state legislatures, and some went to Congress. Many white Southerners accepted the new order, even if unhappily. Others were furious that Black citizens now shared power. That fury soon took the form of a secret order.

words.d: a formal change added to the Constitution
the years 1865 to 1877, when the nation rebuilt the South and decided what freedom would mean
a person who had been enslaved and was now free

look.title: Three Amendments in Five Years
rows: 15th: no denial of the vote by race
look.cite: U.S. Constitution, Amendments XIII-XV; National Archives, The Constitution: Amendments 11-27
look.prompt: How many years passed between the end of slavery and the promise of the vote? How might a former Confederate have felt as each change arrived?

check.q: What did the Fifteenth Amendment do?
choices: It made formerly enslaved people citizens
It said no citizen could be denied the vote because of race
It created the Joint Select Committee
check.why: The reading says the Fifteenth Amendment (1870) said no citizen could be denied the vote because of race. The Thirteenth ended slavery and the Fourteenth made citizens.

check.q: What does Reconstruction mean in this lesson?
choices: The years 1865 to 1877, when the nation rebuilt the South and decided what freedom meant
The rebuilding of Chicago after its great fire
A ceremony used by the Klan
The years just before the Civil War
check.why: The reading defines Reconstruction as the years 1865 to 1877, when the nation rebuilt the South and argued over the meaning of freedom.

check.q: According to the reading, why were some white Southerners furious?
choices: The North raised taxes on cotton
Black citizens now shared political power
check.why: The reading says some white Southerners were furious that Black citizens now shared power.

lessons.title: Six Men in Pulaski
lessons.mainIdea: The Ku Klux began in Pulaski, Tennessee, as a club of six Confederate veterans, though its exact founding date is disputed.
reading: Pulaski is a small town in southern Tennessee. There, six young men formed a club they called the Ku Klux. Each was a Confederate *veteran*, someone who had served as a soldier in the war. The traditional founding date is December 24, 1865. The Tennessee Encyclopedia instead places it in May or early June 1866. Historians have not settled which date is right.

The name is usually traced to the Greek word kuklos, meaning circle. The founders borrowed from the lodges of their day. They used grand titles, costumes and an *initiation*, a ceremony for bringing in a new member. At first they rode around town in disguise, playing at mystery. It looked like one more club among many.

Later, the Klan's defenders described this beginning as a harmless joke that got out of hand. Be careful with that story. It came from people who wanted to excuse what followed. A *primary source* is evidence made at the time, like a letter or sworn testimony. The sworn testimony gathered in 1871 shows organized political terror, not a joke.

words.d: a person who has served as a soldier in the armed forces
a ceremony for bringing a new member into a group
evidence made at the time of an event, such as a letter, a photograph or sworn testimony

look.title: Two Founding Dates
look.text: Account A: The club began on Christmas Eve, December 24, 1865. Account B: The Tennessee Encyclopedia says it began in May or early June 1866. Both accounts agree on the town, Pulaski, Tennessee. Both agree that the founders were six Confederate veterans.
look.prompt: Which facts do both accounts share? What kind of primary source would you need to settle the date?

check.q: Where was the Ku Klux founded?
check.why: The reading says six veterans formed the Ku Klux in Pulaski, a small town in southern Tennessee.

check.q: Why should readers be careful with the story that the Klan began as a harmless joke?
choices: It came from a Supreme Court ruling
It was proven by the 1872 report
It was written by the Klan's victims
It came from people who wanted to excuse the violence that followed
check.why: The reading says the joke story came from people who wanted to excuse what followed, while the 1871 testimony shows organized terror.

check.q: What is an initiation?
choices: A ceremony for bringing in a new member
check.why: The reading defines initiation as a ceremony for bringing in a new member, a form the founders borrowed from lodges.

lessons.title: From Club to Terror Network
lessons.mainIdea: By 1868 the Klan had spread across the South as a loose paramilitary network using terror for political goals.
reading: In April 1867, Klan leaders met in Nashville. They adopted a rulebook called the *Prescript*. It set out ranks with grand titles, from local groups called dens up to a Grand Wizard at the top. Historians widely believe the first Grand Wizard was Nathan Bedford Forrest, a former Confederate general. No membership list survives, so the details of his role are still debated.

The Klan spread across the South in 1867 and 1868. Its dens were only loosely connected. Each local group often acted on its own. What joined them was a shared goal. They meant to stop Black citizens from voting, owning land, going to school and holding office. They also meant to drive out white Republicans who worked with them.

Historians call the Klan a *paramilitary* force. It acted like an army without being an official one. Its members used *terrorism*: violence and threats against ordinary people to reach a political goal. Attacks often rose before elections, when votes were at stake. The Klan was no longer a club. It had become a weapon in a fight over who would rule the South.

words.d: the Klan's rulebook, adopted in 1867, which set out its ranks and titles
organized like an army but not an official army
violence and threats against ordinary people to reach a political goal

look.title: Dots on a Map
look.text: Picture a map of the South in 1868 with small dots scattered across it. Each dot is a local den. The lines between the dots are thin and broken. Yet the dots crowd together in places where Black men are about to vote, or where a Black teacher has just opened a school.
look.prompt: What does the pattern of dots suggest about what drove the violence? Why might loose connections make the Klan harder to stop?

check.q: What was the Prescript?
choices: A federal law against the Klan
check.why: The reading says Klan leaders adopted a rulebook called the Prescript in Nashville in April 1867.

check.q: Why do historians call the Klan a paramilitary force?
choices: It acted like an army without being an official one
It was part of the U.S. Army
check.why: The reading defines paramilitary as acting like an army without being an official one.

check.q: What shared goal joined the Klan's loosely connected dens?
choices: Stopping Black citizens from voting, owning land, schooling and holding office
check.why: The reading says the dens were joined by a goal: stopping Black citizens from voting, owning land, going to school and holding office.

lessons.title: Masks and Night Raids
lessons.mainIdea: Klansmen attacked at night in disguise, using violence as intimidation to frighten whole communities.
reading: Klansmen rode at night. They wore robes, hoods or painted masks. They came to a family's cabin in groups. They dragged people outside, whipped them and sometimes killed them. They burned homes, churches and schools. People called these attacks *night riding*.

A *disguise* did two jobs. It hid who the attackers were, so victims could not easily name them in court. It also spread fear. Yet disguises often failed. Survivors frequently knew the riders by their voices, their horses or their size. Many later named these men to Congress. The riders were not strangers. They were local men, and that made the danger closer.

Historians use the word *intimidation* for threats meant to make people too afraid to act. Night riding was intimidation by design. A family whipped for voting was a warning to every family nearby. The goal was not only to hurt one person. It was to make a whole community stay home on election day.

words.d: attacks by groups of disguised men who came at night
clothing or a mask used to hide who a person is
threats meant to make people too afraid to act

look.title: Two Imagined Witnesses
look.text: These two statements are made up for practice. Witness 1: The men wore masks, but I knew one by his voice and his gray horse. He farms the land next to mine. Witness 2: I could not tell who they were. I only know there were many of them, and they came at midnight.
look.prompt: How could each statement help or hurt a case in court? Why might Witness 1 be in more danger after testifying?

check.q: According to the reading, what two jobs did a disguise do?
choices: It kept riders warm and showed their rank
It paid dues and marked members for the army
It impressed judges and hid weapons
It hid the attackers and spread fear
check.why: The reading says a disguise hid who the attackers were and also spread fear.

check.q: What is intimidation?
choices: Threats meant to make people too afraid to act
check.why: The reading defines intimidation as threats meant to make people too afraid to act.

check.q: Why was a whipping for voting a warning to every family nearby?
choices: It was listed in the Prescript
The goal was to make a whole community afraid to vote
Neighbors were paid to watch it
check.why: The reading says the goal was to make a whole community stay home on election day.

lessons.title: Who Was Targeted
lessons.mainIdea: The Klan attacked the people who stood for the new South: Black voters, officeholders, teachers, and white Republicans.
reading: The Klan's targets had one thing in common. They stood for the new order in the South. Black voters were attacked. So was any Black *officeholder*, a person elected or appointed to a government job. Black ministers, teachers and families who bought land or asked for fair pay were targeted too. Teachers from the North who taught in freedpeople's schools were threatened.

White Southerners who joined the *Republican* Party were targeted as well. The Klan called them traitors. In the South at this time, a Republican usually meant someone who supported Reconstruction and Black voting rights. The parties have changed a great deal since then. So the word meant something different in 1870 than it does today.

Schools drew special anger. Education let freedpeople read contracts, newspapers and ballots. Many Klan attacks burned schoolhouses or drove teachers away. Yet freedpeople kept rebuilding. Families pooled their money to pay teachers and put up new buildings. Their *persistence*, the act of continuing despite danger, is part of this story too.

words.d: a person elected or appointed to a government job
in the South during Reconstruction, usually a supporter of Reconstruction and Black voting rights
continuing to do something despite danger or difficulty

look.title: A Schoolhouse, Rebuilt
look.text: Picture a one-room schoolhouse in the South in 1870. One night it burns. Within a few months, families have raised money for boards and nails. A new teacher arrives. The children walk to class past the ashes of the old building.
look.prompt: What does the rebuilt school tell you about what freedpeople valued? Why would a group like the Klan see a school as a threat?

check.q: In the South during Reconstruction, a Republican was usually someone who...
choices: supported Reconstruction and Black voting rights
check.why: The reading says a Southern Republican at this time usually supported Reconstruction and Black voting rights.

check.q: Why did schools draw the Klan's anger?
choices: Education let freedpeople read contracts, newspapers and ballots
Schools were owned by the Klan
Schools were used as army forts
check.why: The reading says education let freedpeople read contracts, newspapers and ballots.

check.q: What does persistence mean in the reading?
check.why: The reading defines persistence as the act of continuing despite danger, like families who rebuilt their schools.

lessons.title: Secrecy and the Courts
lessons.mainIdea: Secrecy made Klan terror work because it let members escape local courts, so accountability became the heart of the fight.
reading: Secrecy did more than hide faces. Klan members swore to protect one another. When a case reached a local court, a member might sit on the *jury*, the group of citizens who decide a verdict. Other members could supply an *alibi*, a claim that the accused was somewhere else at the time. Some local sheriffs were members or friends of members.

Witnesses faced a terrible choice. Naming an attacker could bring another raid. Many survivors spoke anyway. Others fled their homes, sometimes hiding in the woods for many nights. Local courts so rarely punished the riders that many Black Southerners came to believe only the federal government could protect them.

Here is the key idea of this chapter. A secret order becomes dangerous when secrecy lets its members escape the law. Many lodges of the time kept harmless secrets, like handshakes and passwords. The Klan used the same forms to hide crimes. That is why *accountability*, making people answer for what they do, became the heart of the fight against it.

words.d: a group of citizens who hear a court case and decide the verdict
a claim that an accused person was somewhere else when a crime happened
making people answer for what they do

look.title: Comparing Two Secrets
look.text: Secret A: A lodge member promises not to tell outsiders the handshake used at meetings. Secret B: A group of men promise not to tell a court who burned a neighbor's house. Both secrets are kept by an oath. Both are kept from outsiders.
look.prompt: What makes Secret A harmless and Secret B a danger to the law? Write one sentence that explains the difference.

check.q: What is an alibi?
choices: A claim that the accused was somewhere else at the time
check.why: The reading defines an alibi as a claim that the accused was somewhere else at the time.

check.q: According to the reading, why did many Black Southerners turn to the federal government?
choices: Local courts rarely punished the riders
Their states had no courts at all
check.why: The reading says local courts so rarely punished the riders that many believed only the federal government could protect them.

check.q: What made the Klan's secrecy different from a typical lodge's?
choices: The Klan used secrecy to hide crimes and escape the law
check.why: The reading says lodges kept harmless secrets, while the Klan used the same forms to hide crimes.

lessons.title: Congress Investigates
lessons.mainIdea: In 1871 a Joint Select Committee of Congress took sworn testimony from hundreds of Southerners and printed it in 13 volumes.
reading: In April 1871, Congress created a *Joint Select Committee*, a special group with members from both the House and the Senate. Its job was to study the condition of affairs in the former Confederate states. In plain words, that meant the violence. Its members heard witnesses in Washington. Some of them also traveled to towns across the South.

Witnesses gave *testimony*, statements made under oath. Clerks wrote down their words. Hundreds of people testified: Black and white, farmers and preachers, officials and Klan suspects. Survivors described raids, whippings and killings. Many named the men they recognized, even though speaking up was dangerous.

The committee sent in its report on February 19, 1872. It filled 13 printed *volumes*, from the Government Printing Office. The first volume holds the report itself. Most of the rest is testimony. Today libraries share these volumes free online. They are one of the richest records of ordinary Americans describing political violence in their own words.

words.d: a special committee with members from both the House and the Senate, formed for one task
a statement made under oath
the separate books that make up one large set

look.title: The Committee's Report
look.text: The committee's report fills 13 volumes. The first volume holds the majority report, the minority's views and the committee's journal of its meetings, from April 1871 to February 1872. The other volumes hold sworn testimony from witnesses about conditions in the Southern states.
look.cite: Joint Select Committee to Inquire into the Condition of Affairs in the Late Insurrectionary States, Report, 13 vols. (Government Printing Office, 1872)
look.prompt: Why might it matter that the majority report, the minority views and the testimony were all printed in the same record?

check.q: What was the Joint Select Committee?
choices: A special group with members from both the House and the Senate
A federal court in South Carolina
check.why: The reading defines the Joint Select Committee as a special group with members from both the House and the Senate.

check.q: How many volumes did the committee's report fill?
check.why: The reading says the report filled 13 printed volumes.

check.q: What is testimony?
check.why: The reading defines testimony as statements made under oath.

lessons.title: Elias Hill of York County
lessons.mainIdea: Elias Hill, a disabled Black preacher and teacher, survived a Klan attack, testified, and led his neighbors to a new life in Liberia.
reading: Elias Hill lived in York County, South Carolina. A childhood illness left him unable to walk or use his arms. He grew up to become a Baptist preacher and a schoolteacher. People in his community trusted him to teach their children to read. They trusted him to lead them in worship.

On the night of May 6, 1871, disguised Klansmen came to his cabin. They dragged him outside and beat him. The attack was aimed at a respected Black leader. When members of the congressional committee came to York County that year, Hill chose to *testify*, or give evidence under oath. He described the attack in careful detail.

Hill was a *witness* and a leader, not someone to pity. After the attack, he decided his community could not be safe at home. In the autumn of 1871 he led a group of neighbors who chose to *emigrate*, or move to another country to live. They sailed to Arthington, Liberia, in West Africa. Hill died there in March 1872. His testimony still speaks for him.

words.d: to give evidence under oath
a person who saw or lived through something and tells about it
to leave your country to live in another one

look.title: A Teacher Gives Evidence
look.text: Picture the scene in York County in 1871. Members of a congressional committee sit at a table. Elias Hill, who cannot walk, has come to speak. A clerk dips his pen. Hill begins to tell, clearly and in order, what happened on the night the riders came.
look.prompt: What kind of courage did it take for Hill to testify? What does his testimony give historians that a newspaper story could not?

check.q: What work did Elias Hill do in his community?
choices: He was a sheriff and judge
He was a Baptist preacher and schoolteacher
He was a member of Congress
check.why: The reading says Hill became a Baptist preacher and a schoolteacher in York County.

check.q: Where did Hill lead a group of neighbors in 1871?
check.why: The reading says Hill led neighbors who emigrated to Arthington, Liberia, in the autumn of 1871.

check.q: According to the reading, how should we see Elias Hill?
choices: As a founder of the Klan
As a witness and a leader
check.why: The reading says Hill was a witness and a leader, not someone to pity.

lessons.title: Two Reports, One Record
lessons.mainIdea: The committee split: the majority found an organized conspiracy, and the minority said the danger was overstated.
reading: The committee did not agree. The Republican members formed the majority. Their *majority report* concluded that the Klan was a real, organized *conspiracy*, a secret plan by a group to do something unlawful. It found that the order used violence to overturn elections and deny citizens their rights. The majority supported strong federal action to stop it.

The Democratic members wrote a *minority report*. They argued that the danger had been overstated. They blamed the Reconstruction state governments for much of the disorder. Both reports were printed together in the first volume. The same testimony stood behind both conclusions.

This gives you a real historian's task. When two groups read the same evidence and reach opposite conclusions, go back to the evidence. Ask who had reasons to see it one way. Each side was *partisan*, strongly loyal to its own party. Historians today, reading the hundreds of sworn accounts, widely agree with the majority on the main point: the Klan was organized terror.

words.d: the conclusions of the larger group of members on a committee
the conclusions of the smaller group of committee members who disagree
a secret plan by a group to do something unlawful
strongly loyal to one political party

look.title: Same Evidence, Two Conclusions
look.text: Majority view, in brief: The attacks follow a pattern. They target voters and officeholders, and the riders act together. This is an organized conspiracy. Minority view, in brief: The disorder is real but exaggerated. It grows out of bad government in the Southern states.
look.prompt: What kind of testimony would you look for to test each view? Which pattern in the evidence would be hardest for the minority view to explain?

check.q: What did the majority report conclude?
choices: The Klan was an organized conspiracy that used violence against citizens' rights
The violence was caused by teachers from the North
The Klan should be made legal
check.why: The reading says the majority found the Klan was a real, organized conspiracy that used violence to deny citizens their rights.

check.q: What is a minority report?
choices: The conclusions of the smaller group of committee members who disagree
check.why: The reading says the Democratic members, the smaller group, wrote a minority report that disagreed with the majority.

check.q: What does partisan mean?
choices: Strongly loyal to one political party
check.why: The reading defines partisan as strongly loyal to one's own party.

lessons.title: The Enforcement Acts
lessons.mainIdea: Congress passed three Enforcement Acts in 1870 and 1871, and part of the Ku Klux Klan Act still protects rights today.
reading: Congress passed three *Enforcement Acts* between May 1870 and April 1871. They were meant to enforce the Fourteenth and Fifteenth Amendments. They made it a *federal* crime to use force or threats to keep citizens from voting. A federal crime is one against the laws of the whole nation. Federal courts, not only local ones, could now hear these cases.

The third law, signed on April 20, 1871, is called the Ku Klux Klan Act. It made it a federal crime to *conspire*, or secretly plan together, to deny people their rights. It also let the president suspend *habeas corpus* where the violence was out of control. Habeas corpus is a person's right to be brought before a judge and not held in jail without cause.

One part of that law still works today. Section 1 lets people sue officials who violate their constitutional rights. It is now known as 42 U.S.C. section 1983. In 1961 the Supreme Court relied on it in Monroe v. Pape, a case about Chicago police who searched a family's home without a warrant. A law written against night riders now protects people across the country.

belonging to the national government rather than a state
to secretly plan together to do something unlawful
a person's right to be brought before a judge and not held in jail without cause

lessons.title: Grant and South Carolina
lessons.mainIdea: President Grant suspended habeas corpus in nine South Carolina counties in 1871, leading to arrests and federal trials.
reading: Upstate South Carolina saw some of the worst Klan violence. On October 17, 1871, President Ulysses S. Grant suspended habeas corpus in nine counties there, including York, Spartanburg and Chester. Federal troops and *marshals*, officers who make arrests for the federal courts, moved in. Suspects could now be held for trial without the usual delays.

Hundreds of men were arrested, and many others fled the state. Grant's attorney general, Amos T. Akerman, pushed hard for *prosecution*, the work of bringing criminal charges in court. Federal trials of accused Klansmen were held in South Carolina in 1871 and 1872. Historian Lou Falkner Williams tells their story in a 1996 book.

The trials had real limits. Courts were slow, and only a small share of the accused were ever punished. Still, the arrests broke the Klan's power in much of the South. Survivors had asked for protection, and for a time the federal government answered. It showed that the law could drag a secret order into the open.

words.d: federal officers who make arrests and carry out orders for the federal courts
the work of bringing criminal charges against someone in court
to stop something for a period of time

look.text: President Grant declared that unlawful groups in nine South Carolina counties were resisting the laws and the courts could not stop them. He therefore suspended the privilege of the writ of habeas corpus in those counties, so people arrested for these crimes could be held for trial.
look.cite: Ulysses S. Grant, Proclamation 201, Suspending the Writ of Habeas Corpus in Certain Counties of South Carolina, October 17, 1871 (The American Presidency Project)

lessons.title: The Order Fades, the Terror Stays
lessons.mainIdea: The first Klan broke up by about 1872, but open groups like the White League carried on its goals and Reconstruction ended in 1877.
reading: By about 1872, the Klan as an organized order had largely broken up. Arrests, trials and federal troops did much of that work. But the Klan's goals did not disappear. *White supremacy*, the belief that white people should rule over others, stayed strong in Southern politics.

New groups took the Klan's place. The *White League*, founded in Louisiana in 1874, did not hide. It operated openly, as an armed force backing the Democratic Party there. In South Carolina, armed men called Red Shirts rode openly during the 1876 campaign. Violence and fraud helped these groups take back state governments.

In 1877 the federal government stopped protecting the last Reconstruction governments, and Reconstruction ended. Over the next decades, Southern states found ways to *disfranchise* most Black men. Remember the witnesses, though. Their testimony became part of the national record. Nearly a century later, the civil rights movement drew on the same amendments and laws they had fought for.

words.d: the false belief that white people should rule over people of other races
an armed group founded in Louisiana in 1874 that used violence openly to end Reconstruction
to take away a person's right to vote

chapters.title: The Second Klan and Those Who Exposed It
chapters.bigQuestion: How did the 1920s Klan grow so large, and how did reporters, courts and ordinary people break its hold?

story.title: Names in the Morning Paper
story.kicker: In 1922, a Chicago weekly called Tolerance prints the names of people it says belong to the Klan.
paragraphs: It is 1922 in Chicago. The Ku Klux Klan has come north, and it has come to the city. By one count it will soon have about 50,000 members in the Chicago area, more than any other American city. Members meet in rented halls and in fields at the edge of town. Most keep their membership secret from neighbors and bosses.

A new group, the American Unity League, has decided to fight that secrecy. Most of its members are Catholic. The Klan attacks Catholics, Jews, Black Americans and immigrants. The League's weapon is a weekly paper called Tolerance. Week after week, it prints the names of people it says are Klan members. It adds their addresses and their jobs.

Picture a kitchen table on a weekday morning. A family opens the paper. The father runs his finger down a long column of names. There is a name he knows from the corner store. There is a name from his own street. The family looks out the window at the houses nearby, and nothing looks quite the same.

For a member, being named could cost friends, customers or a job. For a person named by mistake, the cost could be the same. Tolerance had pulled away the Klan's hood of secrecy, just as the Klan's targets hoped. It had also raised a hard question. When is it right to publish a list of names, and what if the list is wrong?
story.think: Was printing the names of Klan members a fair way to fight a secret hate group? What would you want to know before deciding?

lessons.title: The Film and the Mountain
lessons.mainIdea: A 1915 film glorified the first Klan, and that same year William J. Simmons launched a second Klan on Stone Mountain, Georgia.
reading: On February 8, 1915, a long silent film opened in Los Angeles. It was first called The Clansman and was soon renamed The Birth of a Nation. Director D. W. Griffith based it on a novel by Thomas Dixon. The film was *propaganda*. It showed Black citizens of the Reconstruction South as dangers and showed the Klan as heroes who saved the South.

The *NAACP*, a civil rights group founded in 1909, organized protests. Its members picketed theaters and asked cities to ban the film or cut its worst scenes. The film drew huge crowds anyway. It taught millions of viewers a false version of the history you studied in the last chapter.

On Thanksgiving night, November 25, 1915, William J. Simmons led a small group up Stone Mountain, near Atlanta, Georgia. They burned a cross and declared a new Ku Klux Klan. Simmons won a state charter in early December. The film opened in Atlanta on December 6, and he used its fame to recruit. This *revival* is called the second Klan.

words.d: messages made to push people toward a belief, often by twisting the truth
the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People, a civil rights group founded in 1909
bringing something back after it had ended

look.title: Outside the Theater, 1915
look.text: Picture a crowd outside a theater in 1915. Many people buy tickets eagerly. Near the door, a small group holds signs asking the city to stop the film. The poster on the wall shows a hooded rider on a horse, painted as a hero.
look.prompt: What might the ticket buyers believe they are about to learn? What were the protesters trying to protect?

check.why: The reading says Simmons led a group up Stone Mountain on Thanksgiving night, November 25, 1915.

check.why: The reading says the NAACP picketed theaters and asked cities to ban the film or cut its worst scenes.

check.q: What is propaganda?
choices: Messages that push a belief, often by twisting the truth
check.why: The reading calls the film propaganda, defined as messages made to push a belief, often by twisting the truth.

lessons.title: Selling a Secret Order
lessons.mainIdea: From 1920, paid recruiters sold Klan membership like a product, using the familiar look of fraternal lodges.
reading: At first the new Klan grew slowly. In 1920, Simmons hired two *publicists*, Edward Young Clarke and Mary Elizabeth Tyler. A publicist is someone paid to spread the word about a person or product. Their firm was called the Southern Publicity Association. They treated the Klan like a product to sell. Recruiters called Kleagles fanned out across the country.

Each new member paid a $10 joining fee. The recruiter kept part of it as a *commission*, a share of a sale paid to the seller. The rest moved up to leaders above him. Members also bought robes and other goods from the organization. Money flowed upward from every new recruit, which gave recruiters a strong reason to sign up as many people as they could.

The Klan copied the look of *fraternal* lodges, which are brotherhood clubs with rituals. It had a ritual book, passwords and grand titles. Millions of Americans already belonged to lodges and found that style familiar. But the second Klan used the lodge form to spread hatred. Its recruiters told each town it would defend the town against whatever that town feared.

words.d: people paid to spread the word about a person, group or product
a share of a sale paid to the person who made the sale
having to do with a brotherhood or club whose members call each other brothers

look.title: A Recruiter's Pitch
look.text: Imagine a recruiter in 1922 visiting a small-town lodge hall. He does not start with violence. He talks about flag, church and protecting the community. He offers a secret handshake, a robe and the warm feeling of belonging. At the very end, he mentions the $10 fee.
look.prompt: What was the recruiter really selling? Why might a harmful group hide its goals behind friendly words?

Ida B. Wells and Stetson Kennedy

choices: A share of a sale paid to the seller

lessons.title: Targets and Territory
lessons.mainIdea: The second Klan attacked Black Americans, Catholics, Jews and immigrants, and it was strong in Northern cities like Chicago.
reading: The second Klan targeted more groups than the first. It attacked Black Americans, as before. It also attacked Catholics, Jews and immigrants, especially from southern and eastern Europe. This was *nativism*, the belief that people born in a country deserve more rights than newcomers. The Klan also claimed to defend *Prohibition*, the national ban on alcohol, and to police people's private lives.

Many people picture the 1920s Klan as a rural Southern group. The record says otherwise. It was strong in the North and West, in states like Indiana, Oregon, Colorado and Michigan. It was strong in cities like Indianapolis, Detroit, Denver and Chicago. The Encyclopedia of Chicago counts about 50,000 members in the Chicago area, the largest city membership in the nation.

How big was the Klan in all? No reliable national lists survive, so historians must *estimate*. Their estimates run from about 2 million to more than 5 million members at the peak in the mid-1920s. On August 8, 1925, tens of thousands of members marched down Pennsylvania Avenue in Washington, D.C. Many marched with their faces uncovered.

words.d: the belief that people born in a country deserve more rights than newcomers
the national ban on making and selling alcohol, from 1920 to 1933
to make a careful guess about a number when an exact count is not possible

choices: In the North and West, including Indiana and Chicago

lessons.title: The World's Exposé
lessons.mainIdea: The New York World's 1921 exposé revealed the Klan's money and violence, won a Pulitzer Prize, and also helped the Klan grow.
reading: On September 6, 1921, the New York World began a series about the Klan. It ran for 21 days in a row. Editor Herbert Bayard Swope oversaw the project. Reporter Rowland Thomas did much of the digging. Newspapers across the country reprinted the series, so millions of readers saw it.

An *exposé* is a report that reveals hidden wrongdoing. The World printed the Klan's own membership forms. It showed how money from fees moved up to the leaders. It listed violent attacks linked to Klan members, including floggings and tar-and-featherings. The paper won the 1922 *Pulitzer Prize* for Public Service.

Then came a surprise. After the series, Klan membership grew. Klan leaders themselves said the exposé had helped them. For some readers, the stories worked like free advertising. This is a real puzzle for anyone fighting hate. Attention can expose a group, and it can also spread its message. Growth was an *unintended consequence* of the World's work.

words.d: a report that reveals hidden wrongdoing
a top American award for journalism, given each year since 1917
a result that no one planned or wanted

look.title: Two Readers, One Series
look.text: Reader A finishes the World series and writes to her member of Congress, asking for an investigation. Reader B finishes the same series and mails in an application to join the Klan. Both read the same facts about fees, secrets and violence.
look.prompt: Why might the same facts push two readers in opposite directions? What could reporters do to lower the chance of Reader B's reaction?

check.q: What is an exposé?
choices: A report that reveals hidden wrongdoing
check.why: The reading defines an exposé as a report that reveals hidden wrongdoing.

check.q: What award did the World win for the series?
choices: The Pulitzer Prize for Public Service
check.why: The reading says the World won the 1922 Pulitzer Prize for Public Service.

check.q: What unintended consequence followed the exposé?
choices: The World went out of business
check.why: The reading says Klan membership grew after the series, and Klan leaders said the exposé helped them.

lessons.title: The Hearing in Congress
lessons.mainIdea: In 1921 a House committee questioned Simmons, who called the Klan a patriotic fraternal order, but Congress passed no law.
reading: The exposé pushed Congress to act. On October 11, 1921, the House Committee on Rules opened *hearings* on the Klan. A hearing is a meeting where lawmakers question witnesses to gather facts. Reporters from the World and critics of the Klan gave evidence about what they had found.

William J. Simmons testified too. He presented the Klan as a patriotic, law-abiding *fraternal order*, a brotherhood like many other lodges. He denied that the Klan as an organization had ordered the violence in the newspapers. His performance was calm and confident. Many listeners found him convincing.

Congress passed no law against the Klan after the hearings. The printed record, 184 pages from the Government Printing Office, survives today. It lets you set Simmons's *claims* beside the evidence the World gathered. Comparing a group's own story with outside evidence is one of the most important skills a historian has.

words.d: meetings where lawmakers question witnesses to gather facts
a brotherhood or lodge whose members share rituals and help one another
statements that something is true, which may need proof

look.title: Simmons Before the Committee
look.text: Simmons told the committee that the Klan was a patriotic fraternal order that obeyed the law. He denied that the organization had ordered the attacks reported in the press, and he asked the lawmakers to judge it by its stated ideals.
look.cite: U.S. House of Representatives, Committee on Rules, The Ku-Klux Klan: Hearings, 67th Congress, 1st Session (Government Printing Office, 1921)
look.prompt: Which evidence from the World series would you use to test Simmons's claims? What question would you have asked him?

check.why: The reading says the House Committee on Rules opened hearings on October 11, 1921.

check.q: How did Simmons describe the Klan?
choices: As a patriotic, law-abiding fraternal order
check.why: The reading says Simmons presented the Klan as a patriotic, law-abiding fraternal order.

check.q: What did Congress do after the hearings?
choices: It passed no law against the Klan
check.why: The reading says Congress passed no law against the Klan after the hearings.

lessons.title: Chicago's Unity League
lessons.mainIdea: Chicago's American Unity League fought the Klan by printing members' names in its paper Tolerance, which raised hard questions.
reading: In 1922, people in Chicago formed the American Unity League. Most of its members were Roman Catholic. It set out to fight the Klan by breaking its secrecy. Its weekly paper, Tolerance, ran from 1922 into 1923. It printed the names, addresses and jobs of thousands of people it said were Klan members in the Chicago area.

The idea was simple. The Klan depended on secrecy. Its members wanted to keep their friends, customers and jobs while working against their neighbors. Once named in public, they had to face their community. This tactic is called *exposure*: making hidden facts public so people must answer for them.

Exposure is powerful, but it carries risks. A list can contain mistakes. Being named can bring threats or a lost job, whether the name is right or wrong. Today, publishing someone's private information so others can target them is called *doxxing*. People still debate where exposing a hate group ends and unfair harm begins. Your answer shows what you value about *privacy*.

words.d: making hidden facts public so people must answer for them
publishing someone's private information so that others can target them
a person's right to keep some information to themselves

look.text: List 1 is copied from a Klan chapter's own records, and each name is checked twice against other evidence. List 2 is built from rumors that readers mailed in. Both lists are printed in the same newspaper, under the same headline, in the same size type.
look.prompt: Which list would you trust more, and why? Write two rules you would follow before printing any list of names.

choices: Making hidden facts public so people must answer for them
check.why: The reading defines exposure as making hidden facts public so people must answer for them.

lessons.title: The Klan War in Williamson County
lessons.mainIdea: In southern Illinois, Klan-backed liquor raids set off a deadly local war in 1924 and 1925.
reading: Williamson County lies in the coal country of southern Illinois. In the 1920s, Prohibition made alcohol illegal, but a *bootlegger*, someone who makes or sells alcohol against the law, could still find buyers. Beginning in the winter of 1923 to 1924, the Klan backed a series of raids on bootleggers and saloons. A raider named S. Glenn Young led them.

The raids set off a local war. On one side were the Klan and its raiders. Critics called them a *vigilante* force, people taking the law into their own hands. On the other were the sheriff's allies and the Shelton gang of bootleggers. Gunfights broke out in the towns of Herrin and Marion. On January 24, 1925, a shootout in a Herrin cigar store killed four men: Young, Deputy Ora Thomas, and two of Young's companions.

Was it about liquor or about people? The Klan said it was enforcing the law. Critics point out that many of those raided were Italian immigrants and Catholics, groups the Klan attacked everywhere. Historians see more than one *motive* at work. By 1926 the local Klan had lost its power. Keep this separate from the Herrin Massacre of 1922, a deadly mine-strike clash that was not a Klan event.

words.d: a person who makes or sells alcohol against the law
a person who takes the law into his or her own hands without lawful authority
the reason a person or group does something

look.title: Liquor or Prejudice?
look.text: Claim 1: The raids were about enforcing Prohibition, which was the law of the land. Claim 2: The raids were about targeting immigrant and Catholic families the Klan already hated. Both claims were made in the 1920s. Both are still discussed by historians today.
look.prompt: What evidence would support each claim? Could both be partly true? Explain your thinking.

check.why: The reading says a raider named S. Glenn Young led the raids.

check.q: What happened in the Herrin cigar store on January 24, 1925?

check.why: The reading says a shootout there killed Young, Deputy Ora Thomas and two of Young's companions.

check.q: How is the Herrin Massacre of 1922 different from the Klan war?
choices: It was a mine-strike clash, not a Klan event
check.why: The reading says the Herrin Massacre of 1922 was a deadly mine-strike clash that was not a Klan event.

lessons.title: One Woman's Testimony
lessons.mainIdea: Madge Oberholtzer's dying declaration sent Indiana Klan leader D. C. Stephenson to prison for life.
reading: D. C. Stephenson led the Klan in Indiana in the early 1920s. His title was Grand Dragon. Indiana had one of the largest Klans in the nation. Stephenson had great political power, and many officials owed their elections to Klan votes. He presented himself as a champion of law, order and clean living.

In March 1925, Stephenson kidnapped a young woman named Madge Oberholtzer, who worked for the state of Indiana. He violently attacked her. She was badly hurt and died on April 14, 1925. Before she died, she gave a sworn statement about what he had done. A statement like this, made by a person who knows she is dying, is called a *dying declaration*.

The court allowed her statement as evidence. On November 14, 1925, a jury in Noblesville, Indiana, reached its *verdict*. It convicted Stephenson of second-degree murder, and he was sentenced to life in prison. He filed an *appeal*, but in 1932 the Indiana Supreme Court upheld the verdict. Her words broke the most powerful Klan leader in the North.

words.d: a sworn statement by a person who knows he or she is dying, which a court may accept as evidence
the decision a jury reaches at the end of a trial
a request for a higher court to review a trial's decision

look.cite: Stephenson v. State, 205 Ind. 141, 179 N.E. 633 (Indiana Supreme Court, 1932)

check.why: The reading defines a dying declaration as a statement made by a person who knows she is dying.

check.why: The reading says a jury in Noblesville convicted him of second-degree murder, and he was sentenced to life.

check.q: What was Stephenson's title in the Klan?
check.why: The reading says Stephenson led the Klan in Indiana with the title Grand Dragon.

lessons.title: The Fall of the Second Klan
lessons.mainIdea: Scandal, exposure and organized opposition drove the Klan's membership down sharply in the late 1920s.
reading: The Stephenson case shocked many Klan members. The Klan had sold itself as a defender of morals and law. Now its most powerful Northern leader was a convicted murderer. The *scandal*, a public event that causes shock and anger, drove members away. In Indiana they left in large numbers. Elsewhere, fights among leaders over money and power drove others out.

Opposition had been growing too. On May 17, 1924, students from the University of Notre Dame, a Catholic school, went into South Bend, Indiana, to *confront* a Klan rally. Catholic, Jewish and Black groups, newspapers and lawyers kept up the pressure. Some cities and states passed laws against wearing masks in public.

Hiram Evans had replaced Simmons as the Klan's national leader in 1922. He could not stop the fall. By 1930 the Klan was a small shadow of what it had been only five years before. Exposure, courts and organized *civic groups* had broken the hold of a secret order that once counted its members in the millions.

words.d: a public event that causes shock and anger
to face someone or something directly, especially to oppose it
groups of citizens who work together for their community

look.title: Why Did It Fall?

look.prompt: Rank the four factors from most to least important in the Klan's collapse. Support your top choice with evidence from this chapter.

choices: The Klan held its founding meeting

check.q: Why did the Stephenson case hurt the Klan so badly?

It moved the Klan's headquarters to Chicago
check.why: The reading says the Klan sold itself as a defender of morals and law, but its top Northern leader was a convicted murderer.

lessons.title: Ida B. Wells: Facts as a Weapon
lessons.mainIdea: Ida B. Wells used white newspapers' own reports as data to expose the lies behind lynching, and she did it from Chicago.
reading: Ida B. Wells was born into slavery in Holly Springs, Mississippi, in 1862. She became a teacher and then a *journalist*, a person who reports the news, in Memphis, Tennessee. In 1892 a white mob in Memphis killed three Black businessmen. One of them was her friend. Their grocery store had competed with a white-owned store nearby.

Wells began to investigate *lynching*, the killing of a person by a mob without any trial. Many white newspapers claimed lynchings punished terrible crimes. Wells tested that claim. She collected the white newspapers' own reports and checked what the victims had actually been accused of. The claim often fell apart. After she wrote about it, threats kept her from returning to Memphis.

She settled in Chicago, married and raised a family there. In 1895 she published A Red Record in Chicago. It gathered lynching cases and counted them year by year. Her method was to use *data*, facts and numbers collected to answer a question, against a lie. She took part in founding the NAACP in 1909 and worked from Chicago for the rest of her life.

words.d: a person who gathers and reports the news
the killing of a person by a mob without any trial
facts and numbers collected to answer a question

look.title: Wells Explains Her Method
look.text: Wells told readers that her figures did not come from Black sources. She drew them from records kept by white newspapers, so no critic could say she had invented them. With those records she showed how often the crime used to excuse a lynching had not even been charged.
look.cite: Ida B. Wells, A Red Record (Chicago: Donohue and Henneberry, 1895)
look.prompt: Why was it smart to use her opponents' own newspapers? How does that choice make her argument stronger?

check.q: What is lynching?
choices: The killing of a person by a mob without any trial
check.why: The reading defines lynching as the killing of a person by a mob without any trial.

check.q: Where did Wells publish A Red Record in 1895?
check.why: The reading says Wells published A Red Record in Chicago in 1895.

check.q: What was Wells's method?
choices: She used white newspapers' own reports as data to test their claims
check.why: The reading says she collected white newspapers' own reports and checked what victims had actually been accused of.

lessons.title: The NAACP and Its Membership List
lessons.mainIdea: In NAACP v. Alabama (1958), the Supreme Court protected the NAACP's membership list from a state that wanted it.
reading: The NAACP was founded in 1909. It fought lynching and *segregation*, the forced separation of people by race, through courts, research and public pressure. In 1915 it led protests against The Birth of a Nation. Over the next decades, its lawyers won major civil rights cases before the Supreme Court.

In the 1950s, the state of Alabama tried to force the NAACP to hand over its membership lists. Members knew what could happen if their names became public. They could lose jobs, face threats or be attacked. The NAACP refused to give up the names. The case went to the U.S. Supreme Court as NAACP v. Alabama.

On June 30, 1958, the Court ruled *unanimously*, with every justice agreeing, for the NAACP. Justice Harlan wrote the opinion. Alabama could not force the group to reveal its members, because that would expose them to harm and weaken their *freedom of association*, the right to join with others for a shared cause. Notice the twist. A secret list can protect people, not only hide wrongdoing.

words.d: the forced separation of people by race
with every member agreeing
the right to join together with others for a shared cause

look.title: Two Lists of Names
look.text: 1922: A Chicago paper prints the names of people it says belong to the Klan, to break a hate group's secrecy. 1958: The Supreme Court rules that Alabama cannot force the NAACP to reveal its members, to protect them from harm.
look.prompt: Both cases involve a list of members that someone wanted kept secret. What makes the two situations different? Try to write one rule that fits both.

check.q: What did the Supreme Court decide in NAACP v. Alabama (1958)?
choices: The NAACP had to publish its lists
Alabama could not force the NAACP to hand over its membership lists
check.why: The reading says the Court ruled Alabama could not force the NAACP to reveal its members.

check.q: What is freedom of association?
choices: The right to join together with others for a shared cause
The right to a jury trial
The right to a free newspaper
check.why: The reading defines freedom of association as the right to join with others for a shared cause.

check.q: Why did NAACP members want their names kept private?
choices: They had not paid their dues
They could lose jobs, face threats or be attacked
check.why: The reading says members knew they could lose jobs, face threats or be attacked if their names became public.

lessons.title: Stetson Kennedy and the Debate
lessons.mainIdea: Stetson Kennedy's famous story of going undercover in the Klan was later shown to borrow from another informant, and it is still debated.
reading: Stetson Kennedy was a writer from Florida who fought the Klan in the 1940s. He said he went undercover inside the Georgia Klan in 1946 and 1947. He also said he passed its secret words to the makers of the Adventures of Superman radio show. In June 1946 the show aired a 16-episode story called Clan of the Fiery Cross. Young listeners heard Superman defeat a hate group.

The story became famous. In 2005 the best-selling book Freakonomics retold it. Then a researcher named Ben Green found problems. On January 8, 2006, the Freakonomics authors, Steven Levitt and Stephen Dubner, wrote an article called Hoodwinked? in the New York Times Magazine. They reported that much of Kennedy's inside information had come from an *informant* known as John Brown.

Kennedy's defenders answer that he did real, brave work against the Klan. The Superman series is not in doubt. Neither is Georgia's 1947 move to revoke the Klan's state charter. What is still debated is how much Kennedy chose to *embellish*, or add to, his own role. A *memoir* can be both useful and unreliable. Checking it against other records is the historian's job.

words.d: a person who secretly gives information about a group to someone outside it
to add details to a story to make it more exciting, sometimes untrue ones
a person's written account of his or her own life and experiences

look.title: The Authors Correct Themselves
look.text: Levitt and Dubner wrote that Kennedy's own papers showed that much of the inside information he described had come from another man working inside the Klan. They reported this as a correction to the version of the story they had told in their book.
look.cite: Steven D. Levitt and Stephen J. Dubner, Hoodwinked?, New York Times Magazine, January 8, 2006
look.prompt: Why is it unusual, and valuable, when authors publicly correct a story they told? What does it teach about checking sources?

check.q: What was Clan of the Fiery Cross?
choices: A 1946 Superman radio story about defeating a hate group
check.why: The reading says the Adventures of Superman radio show aired this 16-episode story in June 1946.

check.q: What did the 2006 article Hoodwinked? report?
choices: Much of Kennedy's inside information came from an informant
Kennedy had never heard of the Klan
check.why: The reading says Levitt and Dubner reported that much of Kennedy's information came from an informant known as John Brown.

check.q: What does embellish mean?
choices: To add details to a story to make it more exciting
check.why: The reading defines embellish as adding to a story, here Kennedy's own role.

review.q: Which film helped inspire the 1915 revival of the Klan?
review.why: The Birth of a Nation glorified the first Klan in 1915, and Simmons used its fame to recruit.

review.q: Where did William J. Simmons launch the second Klan?
review.why: Simmons and a small group declared the new Klan on Stone Mountain, near Atlanta, on Thanksgiving night 1915.

review.q: What did Chicago's paper Tolerance do?
choices: It printed the names of people it said were Klan members
It reported on Prohibition raids only
review.why: Tolerance, the American Unity League's weekly, printed names, addresses and jobs of people it said were Klan members.

review.q: Why is the growth of the Klan after the World exposé called an unintended consequence?
choices: The World wanted the Klan to grow
Growth was a result no one at the World planned or wanted
The Klan paid for the series
review.why: The World meant to expose the Klan, but the attention also worked like free advertising.

review.q: What role did Madge Oberholtzer's dying declaration play?
choices: It helped convict D. C. Stephenson of murder
It started the Williamson County war
review.why: Her sworn statement was admitted as evidence, and Stephenson was convicted of second-degree murder in 1925.

review.q: How did Ida B. Wells prove that claims about lynching were false?
choices: She used white newspapers' own reports as data
review.why: Wells gathered white newspapers' reports and checked what victims had actually been accused of.

review.q: How do the Tolerance lists and NAACP v. Alabama differ?
choices: Both were decided by the Supreme Court
Tolerance exposed a hate group's members; the Court protected a civil rights group's members
review.why: Tolerance printed names to break the Klan's secrecy, while the 1958 ruling kept NAACP members' names private to protect them.

review.q: Why is Stetson Kennedy's story still debated?
choices: No one knows if the Klan existed in Georgia
Kennedy denied ever writing about the Klan
Much of his inside information came from an informant, and how much he embellished is disputed
review.why: The 2006 article reported an informant was the source of much of his information, while his defenders point to his real anti-Klan work.
